proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(P\) as in the statement and fix \(\widetilde P\in\mathcal F(p)\).  By \(\texttt{ass:cohort-overlap}\), conditioning on either cohort is well defined.  Equality of the observed four-wave cell vector throughout \(\mathcal F(p)\), together with \(\texttt{ass:no-date-one-absorption}\) for \(P\), gives
\[
 \widetilde P(X_1=e\mid D=d)=P(X_1=e\mid D=d)=0.                         \tag{1}
\]
Because \(Z\) has the finite support \(\{1,\ldots,J\}\) by \(\texttt{ass:two-types}\), nonnegativity and (1) imply
\[
 \widetilde P(Z=j,X_1=e\mid D=d)=0                                      \tag{2}
\]
for every \(j,d\).  Hence, using the definitions of \(\pi_j^d\) and \(\alpha_j^d\),
\[
 \widetilde\pi_j^d
 =\widetilde P(Z=j,X_1\in\mathcal A\mid D=d)
 =\widetilde\alpha_j^d.                                                  \tag{3}
\]
The theorem \(\texttt{thm:active-frontier-recovery}\) identifies the right-hand side throughout the fiber and derives its strict positivity from the anchor-star rank condition.  Applying it first to \(P\) and then to \(\widetilde P\) yields
\[
 \widetilde\pi_j^d=\widetilde\alpha_j^d
 =\alpha_j^d=\pi_j^d>0.                                                   \tag{4}
\]

The same theorem recovers the complete unnormalized component law on \(\{X_1\in\mathcal A\}\).  Equations (1)--(4) show that this event has conditional probability one within every positive type--cohort cell.  Therefore the recovered sublaw is the complete component law of \((Z,X_0,X_1,X_2,X_3)\) in each cohort, and division by the positive mass in (4) recovers its type-conditional version.

Let
\[
 \Delta=\operatorname{onehot}(X_3(1))-\operatorname{onehot}(X_3(0)).
\]
By (1)--(4), conditioning additionally on \(X_1\in\mathcal A\) removes a null event inside \(\{D=1,Z=j\}\).  The causal definitions and the active-frontier identity therefore give
\[
 \tau_j=E_P(\Delta\mid D=1,Z=j)
 =E_P(\Delta\mid D=1,Z=j,X_1\in\mathcal A)
 =\eta_j=\frac{\nu_j}{\alpha_j^1}
 =\frac{\nu_j}{\pi_j^1}.                                                  \tag{5}
\]
The aggregate equality \(\tau=\sum_{j=1}^J\nu_j\) and \(\Phi(p)=\theta_J\) are supplied by \(\texttt{thm:active-frontier-recovery}\).  Its construction inverts only selected active-state minors and full-row-rank terminal factors; the absorbing row is fixed by \(\texttt{ass:absorbing-exit}\) and may be rank deficient.  No equality across dates is used, so time homogeneity is unnecessary.  Every input is a marginal of \((D,X_0,X_1,X_2,X_3)\); thus no date beyond \(3\) is required.

First consider the generic pair in \(\texttt{def:outside-face-pair}\).  The construction preserves the cohort probabilities and, conditional on either cohort, gives both allocations the observed four-wave law
\[
 (1-\varepsilon)P^\circ(X_{0:3}\in\cdot\mid D=d)
 +\varepsilon\delta_{(e,e,e,e)}.                                           \tag{1}
\]
Thus the observed law is independent of whether the added atom receives label \(h\) or label \(k\).  The base law has no date-\(1\) absorbers.  By absorption, it consequently has no mass at \(X_0=e\).  Conditional on \((D,Z)\), the retained and added components are separated by the current state until absorption: an active current state can occur only in the retained component, while at \(e\) both components move deterministically to \(e\).  Therefore each marginal potential path remains first-order Markov.  Consistency, no anticipation, absorption, the two common untreated transitions, and cohort overlap are preserved componentwise.

Every active slice and active predecessor mass is multiplied by \(1-\varepsilon\).  Hence each required order-\(J\) determinant is multiplied by \((1-\varepsilon)^J\neq0\).  In the four-factor product defining \(K^d\), the two factors \(1-\varepsilon\) and the two inverse factors \((1-\varepsilon)^{-1}\) cancel, so \(K^d\), its simple spectrum, and its labels are unchanged.  Both laws therefore belong to \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{face}}\).

For every type, the recovered active quantities satisfy
\[
 \alpha_j^d=(1-\varepsilon)\alpha_j^{\circ,d},\qquad
 \nu_j=(1-\varepsilon)\nu_j^\circ,\qquad
 \eta_j=\eta_j^\circ,\qquad
 \tau=(1-\varepsilon)\tau^\circ.                                         \tag{2}
\]
The added all-exit path has zero causal contrast.  If \(a_j\in\{0,1\}\) indicates that type \(j\) receives the added mass, then the definitions of full type share, contribution, and conditional effect give
\[
 \pi_j^d=(1-\varepsilon)\pi_j^{\circ,d}+\varepsilon a_j,
 \qquad
 \tau_j=\frac{(1-\varepsilon)\nu_j^\circ}
 {(1-\varepsilon)\pi_j^{\circ,1}+\varepsilon a_j}.                       \tag{3}
\]
The denominator is positive because \(\texttt{thm:active-frontier-recovery}\) derives \(\pi_j^{\circ,d}>0\).  Thus reallocating the atom changes the shares of \(h\) and \(k\), and changes the full conditional effect of each reallocated type whose contribution is nonzero, while preserving all active targets and the aggregate between the two allocations.

We now verify the exact law in \(\texttt{def:exact-witness}\).  Direct row addition gives
\[
 H_j\mathbf1_3=Q_j\mathbf1_3=V_j\mathbf1_3=\mathbf1_3,
 \qquad H_j[e,:]=Q_j[e,:]=V_j[e,:]=(0,0,1),                               \tag{4}
\]
and every entry is nonnegative.  Successive summation of the displayed four-wave atom mass over \(u_0,u_1,s_2,s_1,s_0,j,d\) gives one.  The shared coordinates through date \(2\) establish no anticipation, and \(X_t=X_t(D)\) establishes consistency.  Marginalizing the unused continuation gives the Markov factorizations \((H_j,Q_j,Q_j)\) and \((H_j,Q_j,V_j)\).  Equation (4) establishes absorption.  Moreover,
\[
 P(D=d)=\frac12,\qquad P(Z=j\mid D=d)=\frac12,                             \tag{5}
\]
so the latent support is exactly \(\{1,2\}\), cohort overlap holds, and the common untreated kernels are \(Q_j\).  The active rows of \(H_j\) have zero exit probability, whence \(P(X_1=e\mid D=d)=0\).

The predecessor factors are
\[
 B_a=\begin{pmatrix}3/16&1/12\\1/16&1/6\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 B_b=\begin{pmatrix}1/16&1/6\\3/16&1/12\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad \det B_a=\frac5{192},\quad \det B_b=-\frac5{192}.                \tag{6}
\]
For row \(j\) of \(C_y^0\) use row \(y\) of \(Q_j\), and for row \(j\) of \(C_y^1\) use row \(y\) of \(V_j\).  Direct determinant calculation gives
\[
 \det C_a^{0,\mathcal A}=\frac9{50},\quad
 \det C_b^{0,\mathcal A}=-\frac3{100},\quad
 \det C_a^{1,\mathcal A}=\frac{31}{100},\quad
 \det C_b^{1,\mathcal A}=-\frac1{20}.                                    \tag{7}
\]
By the factorization proved in \(\texttt{thm:active-frontier-recovery}\),
\[
 \det M_{xy}^d=\det(B_x)Q_1[x,y]Q_2[x,y]\det(C_y^{d,\mathcal A}).         \tag{8}
\]
The determinants in the order \((aa,ab,ba,bb)\) are
\[
 \left(\frac9{16000},-\frac3{32000},-\frac9{32000},\frac3{12800}\right) \tag{9}
\]
for cohort \(0\), and
\[
 \left(\frac{31}{32000},-\frac1{6400},-\frac{31}{64000},\frac1{2560}\right) \tag{10}
\]
for cohort \(1\).  Thus every required anchor-star minor is nonsingular.  The cycle diagonal is
\[
 \operatorname{diag}\left(
 \frac{(3/5)(1/2)}{(1/5)(3/10)},
 \frac{(1/5)(3/5)}{(3/10)(2/5)}\right)=\operatorname{diag}(5,1).           \tag{11}
\]
Conjugating by \(B_a\) gives
\[
 K^0=K^1=\begin{pmatrix}29/5&-12/5\\8/5&1/5\end{pmatrix}.                \tag{12}
\]
Its trace is \(6\) and its determinant is \(5\), so its characteristic polynomial is \((\lambda-5)(\lambda-1)\).  Equations (4)--(12) verify every condition defining \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{face}}\), as well as no date-\(1\) absorption.

The row vector \((1/2,1/2,0)\) is invariant under each \(H_j\).  Hence the type-specific date-\(2\) laws in the treated cohort are
\[
 p_{2,1}=(2/5,2/5,1/5),\qquad p_{2,2}=(1/4,1/2,1/4).                       \tag{13}
\]
The constructed potential paths share \(X_2\).  Conditional iterated expectation under that coupling therefore proves the causal identity \(\tau_j=p_{2,j}(V_j-Q_j)\).  Multiplication gives
\[
 \tau_1=(1/25,0,-1/25),\qquad
 \tau_2=(-1/40,-1/40,1/20).                                                \tag{14}
\]
Using the equal type masses in (5),
\[
 \tau=(3/400,-1/80,1/200),\qquad
 \nu_1=(1/50,0,-1/50),\qquad
 \nu_2=(-1/80,-1/80,1/40).                                                 \tag{15}
\]
The absence of date-\(1\) absorption gives \(\alpha_j^d=1/2\) and \(\eta_j=\tau_j\).

Finally apply (1)--(3) with \(\varepsilon=1/5\), \(h=1\), \(k=2\), and (14)--(15).  The common active masses are \((4/5)(1/2)=2/5\), whereas the full shares are \((3/5,2/5)\) under \(P^A\) and \((2/5,3/5)\) under \(P^B\).  Direct substitution gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \tau_1^A&=(2/75,0,-2/75),&
 \tau_2^A&=(-1/40,-1/40,1/20),\\
 \tau_1^B&=(1/25,0,-1/25),&
 \tau_2^B&=(-1/60,-1/60,1/30),
\end{aligned}                                                              \tag{16}
\]
and, under both laws,
\[
 \nu_1=(2/125,0,-2/125),\qquad
 \nu_2=(-1/100,-1/100,1/50),\qquad
 \tau=(3/500,-1/100,1/250).                                                \tag{17}
\]
Equations (1)--(3) show observational equivalence and equality of every active target, while (16) shows the asserted difference in full conditional effects.  This proves both the generic obstruction and every exact numerical claim.

Fix \(P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{face}}\) and \(d\in\{0,1\}\).  Assumption \(\texttt{ass:cohort-overlap}\) gives \(P(D=d)>0\), so every cohort-conditional probability below is defined.  For \(x,y\in\mathcal A\), the factors in \(\texttt{def:observed-slices}\) have dimensions
\[
 B_x^{d,\mathcal A}\in\mathbb R_+^{m\times J},\qquad
 D_{xy}\in\mathbb R_+^{J\times J},\qquad
 C_y^d\in\mathbb R_+^{J\times(m+1)},                                    \tag{1}
\]
and stochasticity gives \(C_y^d\mathbf1_{m+1}=\mathbf1_J\).  By \(\texttt{ass:consistency}\) and \(\texttt{ass:no-anticipation}\), the observed coordinates through date \(2\) equal the corresponding coordinates of the realized potential path.  The conditional first-order Markov factorization in \(\texttt{ass:markov-paths}\), and the common date-two transition in \(\texttt{ass:common-date-two-transition}\), give, for \(u,x,y\in\mathcal A\) and \(v\in\mathcal S\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
 A_{xy}^d[u,v]
 &=\sum_{j=1}^J P(X_0=u,X_1=x,Z=j\mid D=d)
 Q_j[x,y]P(X_3=v\mid X_2=y,Z=j,D=d)\\
 &=\sum_{j=1}^J B_x^{d,\mathcal A}[u,j]Q_j[x,y]C_y^d[j,v].
\end{aligned}                                                              \tag{2}
\]
Thus
\[
 A_{xy}^d=B_x^{d,\mathcal A}D_{xy}C_y^d,
 \qquad M_{xy}^d=B_x^{d,\mathcal U}D_{xy}C_y^{d,\mathcal V}.              \tag{3}
\]

Every factor in the second equality of (3) is square of order \(J\).  Assumption \(\texttt{ass:four-slice-rank}\) makes \(M_{x_0y}^d\) nonsingular for every \(y\in\mathcal A\).  The determinant product in (3) therefore makes \(B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}\), every \(D_{x_0y}\), and every \(C_y^{d,\mathcal V}\) nonsingular.  The same assumption makes \(M_{xy_0}^d\) nonsingular for every \(x\in\mathcal A\), whence every \(B_x^{d,\mathcal U}\) and every \(D_{xy_0}\) is nonsingular.  Since diagonal entries of \(D_{xy}\) are transition probabilities,
\[
 Q_j[x_0,y]>0,\qquad Q_j[x,y_0]>0                                         \tag{4}
\]
for all \(j,x,y\).  These inequalities justify all divisions below.  Notice that \(M_{x_1y_1}^d\) is multiplied but never inverted.

Substitution of (3) into the definition of \(K^d\), followed by cancellation of adjacent invertible factors, yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
 K^d
 &=B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}D_{x_0y_0}C_{y_0}^{d,\mathcal V}
 (B_{x_1}^{d,\mathcal U}D_{x_1y_0}C_{y_0}^{d,\mathcal V})^{-1}\\
 &\quad\cdot B_{x_1}^{d,\mathcal U}D_{x_1y_1}C_{y_1}^{d,\mathcal V}
 (B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}D_{x_0y_1}C_{y_1}^{d,\mathcal V})^{-1}\\
 &=B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}\operatorname{diag}_{1\leq j\leq J}
 \left\{\frac{Q_j[x_0,y_0]Q_j[x_1,y_1]}
 {Q_j[x_1,y_0]Q_j[x_0,y_1]}\right\}
 (B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U})^{-1}.
\end{aligned}                                                              \tag{5}
\]
The displayed cross-ratios are the eigenvalues \(\rho_j^d\).  They are distinct and decreasingly labelled by \(\texttt{ass:simple-cycle-spectrum}\).  If \(E_j\) is diagonal with sole nonzero entry \(E_j[j,j]=1\), direct evaluation of the Lagrange polynomial at the diagonal matrix in (5) proves
\[
 P_j^d=\prod_{k\ne j}\frac{K^d-\rho_k^dI_J}{\rho_j^d-\rho_k^d}
 =B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}E_j(B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U})^{-1}.                  \tag{6}
\]
Summing the latent label in the definition of the observed predecessor vector gives
\[
 m_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}=B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}\mathbf1_J.
\]
Combining this equality with (6) fixes both eigenvector scale and sign:
\[
 P_j^dm_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}=B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}[:,j].                 \tag{7}
\]
Consequently the first matrix built by \(\texttt{def:recovery-map}\) is the true \(B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}\).

Equations (2), (4), and (7) imply, for every \(y\in\mathcal A\),
\[
 F_y^d=D_{x_0y}C_y^d,\qquad
 q_{x_0y}^d=F_y^d\mathbf1_{m+1}=D_{x_0y}\mathbf1_J.                       \tag{8}
\]
Every coordinate of the last vector is positive by (4); hence row-sum normalization gives exactly
\[
 \operatorname{diag}(q_{x_0y}^d)^{-1}F_y^d=C_y^d.                         \tag{9}
\]
The selected minor \(C_{y_0}^{d,\mathcal V}\) is nonsingular, so \(C_{y_0}^d\) has row rank \(J\), and therefore \(C_{y_0}^d(C_{y_0}^d)^\top\) is positive definite.  It follows from (2) and (9) that
\[
\begin{aligned}
 W_x^d
 &=A_{xy_0}^{d,\mathcal U,\mathcal S}(C_{y_0}^d)^\top
 \{C_{y_0}^d(C_{y_0}^d)^\top\}^{-1}\\
 &=B_x^{d,\mathcal U}D_{xy_0}.
\end{aligned}                                                              \tag{10}
\]
This matrix is nonsingular.  Since \(m_x^{d,\mathcal U}=B_x^{d,\mathcal U}\mathbf1_J\),
\[
 c_x^d=(W_x^d)^{-1}m_x^{d,\mathcal U}=D_{xy_0}^{-1}\mathbf1_J>0,
 \qquad W_x^d\operatorname{diag}(c_x^d)=B_x^{d,\mathcal U}.              \tag{11}
\]

When \(J<m\), the selected rows alone do not contain all predecessor masses.  Restricting (2) to rows \(\mathcal A\) and columns \(\mathcal V\), then using (9) and (11), gives the required full-row transport:
\[
\begin{aligned}
 A_{xy_0}^{d,\mathcal A,\mathcal V}(C_{y_0}^{d,\mathcal V})^{-1}
 \operatorname{diag}(c_x^d)
 &=B_x^{d,\mathcal A}D_{xy_0}\operatorname{diag}(c_x^d)\\
 &=B_x^{d,\mathcal A}.
\end{aligned}                                                              \tag{12}
\]
For arbitrary \(x,y\in\mathcal A\), equations (2), (9), and (11) now give
\[
 q_{xy}^d=(B_x^{d,\mathcal U})^{-1}
 A_{xy}^{d,\mathcal U,\mathcal S}\mathbf1_{m+1}
 =D_{xy}\mathbf1_J.                                                        \tag{13}
\]
Thus \(q_{xy}^d[j]=Q_j[x,y]\), including possibly zero non-anchor transitions.  Row stochasticity identifies
\[
 Q_j[x,e]=1-\sum_{y\in\mathcal A}Q_j[x,y],                                \tag{14}
\]
and \(\texttt{ass:absorbing-exit}\) supplies the absorbing exit row.  Equation (9) identifies every active row of the factual first-post matrix \(R_j^d\), and absorption again supplies its exit row.

Summing the recovered predecessor probabilities gives
\[
 s_j^d[x]=\mathbf1_m^\top B_x^{d,\mathcal A}[:,j]
 =P(Z=j,X_1=x\mid D=d),\qquad
 \alpha_j^d=\sum_{x\in\mathcal A}s_j^d[x].                              \tag{15}
\]
The nonnegative square matrix \(B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}\) is nonsingular, so each of its columns is nonzero and has strictly positive column sum.  Consequently
\[
 \alpha_j^d\geq\mathbf1_J^\top B_{x_0}^{d,\mathcal U}[:,j]>0,
 \qquad
 \pi_j^d=\alpha_j^d+P(Z=j,X_1=e\mid D=d)\geq\alpha_j^d>0.                \tag{16}
\]
Thus type overlap is a consequence of the observable rank hypothesis rather than an additional assumption.

Equations (2) and (8)--(15) recover the complete unnormalized component law on \(\{X_1\in\mathcal A\}\).  Indeed, \(\texttt{ass:absorbing-exit}\) implies \(X_1\in\mathcal A\Rightarrow X_0\in\mathcal A\), and for \(u,x,y\in\mathcal A\), \(v\in\mathcal S\), its conditional-on-cohort cell mass is
\[
 B_x^{d,\mathcal A}[u,j]Q_j[x,y]R_j^d[y,v],                               \tag{17}
\]
whereas for \(y=e\) it is
\[
 B_x^{d,\mathcal A}[u,j]Q_j[x,e]\mathbf1\{v=e\}.
\]
In particular, positivity in (16) makes the following conditional law well defined:
\[
 P(X_2\in\cdot\mid D=d,Z=j,X_1\in\mathcal A)
 =\frac{s_j^dQ_j}{\alpha_j^d}.                                             \tag{18}
\]

Because the cross-ratios in (5) involve only the cohort-common matrices \(Q_j\), their strict descending order is common across cohorts.  By consistency, \(R_j^0=U_j\) on active rows.  No anticipation makes the treated cohort's \(X_2\) the same under both potential paths, while \(\texttt{ass:common-first-post-untreated-transition}\) makes its untreated continuation equal to \(U_j=R_j^0\).  If \(X_1=e\), no anticipation and absorption imply \(X_3(1)=X_3(0)=e\), so this event contributes zero.  Iterated expectation using (18) therefore proves the causal, rather than definitional, identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \nu_j
 &=E\!\left[\mathbf1\{Z=j\}
 \{\operatorname{onehot}(X_3(1))-\operatorname{onehot}(X_3(0))\}
 \mid D=1\right]\\
 &=s_j^1Q_j(R_j^1-R_j^0).
\end{aligned}                                                              \tag{19}
\]
Since \(\alpha_j^1>0\), the same calculation conditional on the active event yields
\[
 \eta_j=\frac{\nu_j}{\alpha_j^1}.                                         \tag{20}
\]
Finite additivity over the known support \(Z\in\{1,\ldots,J\}\) gives
\[
 \tau=\sum_{j=1}^J\nu_j.                                                   \tag{21}
\]
Equations (19)--(21) are exactly \(\Phi(p)=\theta_J\).  Every operation used only the observed four-wave law and the declared nonzero ranks, eigengaps, and stochastic normalizations, so the same derivation holds for every \(\widetilde P\in\mathcal F(p)\).  The four matrices occurring in (5) determine the spectral basis; the \(2m-1\) distinct selected anchor-star slices in (8)--(13) transport that basis to all active states.  Neither time homogeneity nor a transition after date \(3\) was used.  Only the four waves \(X_0,\ldots,X_3\) are required; an observed fifth wave may be marginalized out.

Let \(q_d(p)=\sum_{s:D(s)=d}p_s\).  Assumption \(\texttt{ass:cohort-overlap}\) gives \(q_d(p)>0\).  Every entry of \(A_{xy}^d\) and \(m_x^d\) is a linear marginal of the \(N_m\)-cell four-wave vector \(p\), divided by \(q_d(p)\), and is therefore real analytic near a regular law.  The proof of \(\texttt{thm:active-frontier-recovery}\) shows that each inverse and scalar division in \(\Phi\) has a nonzero determinant or denominator there.

We verify analyticity of the spectral step without imposing symmetry.  Fix a regular matrix \(K_0\), and surround each of its distinct real eigenvalues by a disjoint positively oriented complex circle \(\gamma_j\).  Uniformly for \(z\in\gamma_j\) and all sufficiently small real perturbations \(E\),
\[
 (zI_J-K_0-E)^{-1}
 =\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\{(zI_J-K_0)^{-1}E\}^r(zI_J-K_0)^{-1}.               \tag{1}
\]
This Neumann series converges uniformly because the circles are compact subsets of the resolvent set of \(K_0\).  Termwise integration shows that
\[
 \mathcal P_j(K_0+E)=\frac{1}{2\pi\mathrm i}
 \int_{\gamma_j}(zI_J-K_0-E)^{-1}\,dz                                    \tag{2}
\]
is a convergent power series in the entries of \(E\).  Since a matrix with distinct eigenvalues is diagonalizable, substituting its partial-fraction resolvent into (2) shows directly that \(\mathcal P_j\) equals its rank-one Lagrange projector.  Moreover,
\[
 \rho_j(K)=\operatorname{tr}\{K\mathcal P_j(K)\}                         \tag{3}
\]
is the unique eigenvalue inside \(\gamma_j\) and is analytic.  For real \(K\) near \(K_0\), uniqueness inside the circle and conjugate pairing imply that \(\rho_j(K)\) remains real; shrinking the neighborhood preserves the descending order.  Thus the polynomial expression
\[
 P_j=\prod_{k\ne j}\frac{K-\rho_kI_J}{\rho_j-\rho_k}                   \tag{4}
\]
is real analytic wherever the spectrum is simple.  Matrix inversion is analytic by its adjugate-over-determinant formula, and
\[
 C^\dagger=C^\top(CC^\top)^{-1}                                          \tag{5}
\]
is analytic wherever \(C\) has full row rank.  Therefore the finite composition in \(\texttt{def:recovery-map}\) extends real analytically to a relative open neighborhood in the affine hyperplane \(\mathbf1^\top p=1\).

For completeness, its Jacobian is computable by the following recurrence.  Let \(h\) be an affine tangent direction, so \(\mathbf1^\top h=0\), and use a dot for the directional derivative.  Cohort conditioning gives
\[
 \dot q_d=\sum_{s:D(s)=d}h_s,\qquad
 \frac{d}{d\epsilon}\left.
 \frac{p_s+\epsilon h_s}{q_d(p+\epsilon h)}\right|_{\epsilon=0}
 =\frac{h_s}{q_d}-\frac{p_s\dot q_d}{q_d^2}.                              \tag{6}
\]
For every invertible matrix, differentiating \(MM^{-1}=I\) gives \(\dot M^{-1}=-M^{-1}\dot M M^{-1}\).  Differentiating the spectral identities gives
\[
 \dot\rho_j=\operatorname{tr}(P_j\dot K),\qquad
 \dot P_j=\sum_{k\ne j}
 \frac{P_k\dot K P_j+P_j\dot K P_k}{\rho_j-\rho_k}.                    \tag{7}
\]
The first recovery stages satisfy
\[
 \dot B_{x_0}^{\mathcal U}[:,j]
 =\dot P_jm_{x_0}^{\mathcal U}+P_j\dot m_{x_0}^{\mathcal U},
 \quad
 \dot F_y=-B_{x_0}^{-1}\dot B_{x_0}F_y+B_{x_0}^{-1}\dot A_{x_0y},
 \quad \dot q_{x_0y}=\dot F_y\mathbf1_{m+1},                              \tag{8}
\]
and row normalization gives
\[
 \dot C_y[j,:]
 =\frac{\dot F_y[j,:]-\dot q_{x_0y}[j]C_y[j,:]}{q_{x_0y}[j]}.             \tag{9}
\]
Writing \(N=(C_{y_0}C_{y_0}^\top)^{-1}\), differentiation of (5) gives
\[
 \dot C_{y_0}^\dagger
 =\dot C_{y_0}^\top N-C_{y_0}^\top N
 (\dot C_{y_0}C_{y_0}^\top+C_{y_0}\dot C_{y_0}^\top)N.                 \tag{10}
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \dot W_x=\dot A_{xy_0}C_{y_0}^\dagger+A_{xy_0}\dot C_{y_0}^\dagger,
 \quad
 \dot c_x=W_x^{-1}(\dot m_x-\dot W_xc_x),                                \tag{11}
\]
\[
 \dot B_x^{\mathcal U}
 =\dot W_x\operatorname{diag}(c_x)+W_x\operatorname{diag}(\dot c_x).     \tag{12}
\]
The product rule applied to
\[
 B_x^{\mathcal A}=A_{xy_0}^{\mathcal A,\mathcal V}
 (C_{y_0}^{\mathcal V})^{-1}\operatorname{diag}(c_x)
\]
and then to the recovered \(Q_j,R_j^d,s_j^d\) supplies their derivatives.  Finally,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \dot\nu_j
 &=\dot s_j^1Q_j(R_j^1-R_j^0)+s_j^1\dot Q_j(R_j^1-R_j^0)\\
 &\quad+s_j^1Q_j(\dot R_j^1-\dot R_j^0),
 \qquad \dot\tau=\sum_{j=1}^J\dot\nu_j.
\end{aligned}                                                              \tag{13}
\]
Equations (6)--(13) determine \(J_\Phi(p)h\) and include the derivative of every recovered active mass.

Let \(\mathcal S_0\) be the actual finite support stratum and suppose \(p_s>0\) for every \(s\in\mathcal S_0\).  The tangent scores of the saturated multinomial model are exactly the functions \(a\) with \(E_Pa(O)=0\): for every such bounded function, \(p_{\epsilon,s}=p_s\{1+\epsilon a(s)\}\) is a probability vector for sufficiently small \(|\epsilon|\).  Along this path,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \left.\frac{d}{d\epsilon}\Phi(p_\epsilon)\right|_{0}
 &=J_\Phi(p)\sum_{s\in\mathcal S_0}p_se_sa(s)\\
 &=E_P\!\left[J_\Phi(p)(e_O-p)a(O)\right]
 =E_P\{G_p(O)a(O)\}.
\end{aligned}                                                              \tag{14}
\]
Also \(E_PG_p(O)=0\).  Since the saturated tangent space is all of \(L_2^0(P)\), (14) proves that \(G_p\) is the canonical gradient.  Its covariance is
\[
 E_P[G_p(O)G_p(O)^\top]
 =J_\Phi(p)\{\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^\top\}J_\Phi(p)^\top
 =\Sigma(p).                                                               \tag{15}
\]
If a centered influence vector \(H\) represents the same derivative, then (14) implies \(E_P\{(H-G_p)a\}=0\) for every \(a\in L_2^0(P)\).  Taking each coordinate of \(H-G_p\) as a score gives \(H=G_p\) almost surely.  Thus (15) is the saturated information bound.

Assumption \(\texttt{ass:iid-panels}\) gives the exact identity
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat p-p)=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n(e_{O_i}-p).                   \tag{16}
\]
Taylor expansion of the analytic map, together with \(\Phi(p)=\theta_J\) from \(\texttt{thm:active-frontier-recovery}\), yields
\[
 \sqrt n\{\Phi(\widehat p)-\Phi(p)\}
 =n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nG_p(O_i)+o_P(1).                                    \tag{17}
\]
The finite-support summands are centered and bounded.  For every fixed vector \(u\), their characteristic function has the expansion
\[
 E_P\exp\{\mathrm i u^\top G_p(O)/\sqrt n\}
 =1-\frac{u^\top\Sigma(p)u}{2n}+O(n^{-3/2}).                              \tag{18}
\]
Raising (18) to the \(n\)-th power gives the characteristic function of \(N(0,\Sigma(p))\), including when \(\Sigma(p)\) is singular.  The same calculation along a differentiable local multinomial path, combined with Taylor expansion, supplies the deterministic derivative shift and proves regularity on the stratum.  The empirical guard accepts with probability tending to one at every regular law because all finitely many population margins are strictly positive and \(\widehat p\to p\).  Hence the guarded empirical-cell plug-in has influence function \(G_p\) and attains the saturated finite-multinomial information bound.  No efficiency assertion is made for the smaller restricted Markov observed-law image.

Let \(\mathcal K_\kappa\) be the set of \(N_m\)-cell four-wave vectors induced by \(\mathcal P_\kappa\).  It is compact by \(\texttt{def:buffered-class}\).  The finite vector in \(\texttt{def:margin-vector}\) contains every determinant, singular value, eigengap, normalization, division, and label margin used by \(\Phi\), and \(\texttt{ass:variance-buffer}\) controls every reported diagonal.  Population margins are at least \(2\kappa\), whereas the sequential empirical guard stops at \(\kappa\).

Analyticity from \(\texttt{thm:analytic-gradient}\), continuity of the finite margin list, and compactness give \(r>0\) such that the relative closed \(r\)-neighborhood of \(\mathcal K_\kappa\) lies in the analytic recovery domain and passes every algebraic and variance guard at level \(\kappa\).  On that compact neighborhood there are finite constants
\[
 L_1=\sup_q\|J_\Phi(q)\|<\infty,
 \qquad L_2=\sup_q\|D^2\Phi(q)\|<\infty.                                \tag{1}
\]
The empirical vector has legal absorbing support almost surely.  By \(\texttt{ass:iid-panels}\), direct multinomial calculation gives
\[
 E_P\|\widehat p-p\|_2^2
 =\frac{1-\|p\|_2^2}{n}\leq\frac1n.
\]
Markov's inequality therefore gives the uniform bound
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_\kappa}
 P(\|\widehat p-p\|_2>r)\leq\frac1{nr^2}.                                \tag{2}
\]
This proves \(\inf_{P\in\mathcal P_\kappa}P(\mathcal E_\kappa)\to1\), including the buffered empirical variance check.

Taylor's formula on the complement of the event in (2) gives
\[
 \left\|\sqrt n\{\Phi(\widehat p)-\Phi(p)
 -J_\Phi(p)(\widehat p-p)\}\right\|
 \leq\frac{L_2}{2}\sqrt n\|\widehat p-p\|_2^2.                           \tag{3}
\]
For every \(\epsilon>0\), Markov's inequality and the preceding second-moment formula bound the probability that the right side exceeds \(\epsilon\) by \(L_2/(2\epsilon\sqrt n)\), uniformly over the class.  Combining (3), the exact empirical-cell identity, and \(\Phi(p)=\theta_J\) from \(\texttt{thm:active-frontier-recovery}\) proves
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\theta-\theta_J)
 =n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nG_p(O_i)+o_P(1)                                     \tag{4}
\]
uniformly over \(P\in\mathcal P_\kappa\).

From the definition of \(\widehat G_i\), the empirical covariance has the exact finite-multinomial form
\[
 \widehat\Sigma=J_\Phi(\widehat p)
 \{\operatorname{diag}(\widehat p)-\widehat p\widehat p^\top\}
 J_\Phi(\widehat p)^\top.                                                  \tag{5}
\]
The right side is uniformly continuous on the compact neighborhood used in (1).  Equation (2) therefore proves \(\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma(p)=o_P(1)\) uniformly.  In particular, every reported empirical diagonal exceeds \(\kappa\) with probability tending to one uniformly.  No covariance inverse is used.

It remains to prove simultaneous coverage when the correlation matrix is singular.  Take an arbitrary sequence \(P_n\in\mathcal P_\kappa\).  Compactness supplies a subsequence, retained in the notation, for which \(p_n\to p_\star\); continuity gives \(\Sigma(p_n)\to\Sigma(p_\star)\).  For \(\ell\in\mathcal L\), define
\[
 \sigma_{n,\ell}^2=\Sigma_{\ell\ell}(p_n)\geq2\kappa,
 \qquad Y_{n,i,\ell}=G_{p_n,\ell}(O_i)/\sigma_{n,\ell}.                  \tag{6}
\]
The vectors \(Y_{n,i}\) are centered and uniformly bounded by (1) and the diagonal buffer.  After a further subsequence, their positive-semidefinite unit-diagonal correlation matrices \(\Gamma_n\) converge to a positive-semidefinite unit-diagonal matrix \(\Gamma_\star\), which may be singular.  For every fixed vector \(u\), boundedness permits a third-order Taylor expansion with a uniform remainder:
\[
 E_{P_n}\exp\{\mathrm i u^\top Y_{n,1}/\sqrt n\}
 =1-\frac{u^\top\Gamma_nu}{2n}+O(n^{-3/2}).                               \tag{7}
\]
Independence raises (7) to the \(n\)-th power, which converges to \(\exp(-u^\top\Gamma_\star u/2)\).  Hence
\[
 n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nY_{n,i}\ \Longrightarrow\
 Z_\star\sim N(0,\Gamma_\star),                                         \tag{8}
\]
including singular \(\Gamma_\star\).

Conditionally on the sample, the multiplier numerator is exactly Gaussian.  On \(\mathcal E_\kappa\), its studentized correlation is
\[
 \widehat\Gamma_{\ell k}
 =\frac{\widehat\Sigma_{\ell k}}
 {\sqrt{\widehat\Sigma_{\ell\ell}\widehat\Sigma_{kk}}}.               \tag{9}
\]
Covariance consistency and the positive diagonal imply \(\widehat\Gamma\to\Gamma_\star\) in \(P_n\)-probability.  The already established \(\texttt{lem:gaussian-max-quantile-continuity}\) applies to positive-semidefinite unit-diagonal matrices, including singular limits.  If \(c_\star\) is the \((1-\alpha)\)-quantile of \(\max_{\ell\in\mathcal L}|Z_{\star,\ell}|\), then
\[
 \widehat c_{1-\alpha}\to c_\star,
 \qquad
 P\!\left(\max_{\ell\in\mathcal L}|Z_{\star,\ell}|\leq c_\star\right)
 =1-\alpha.                                                               \tag{10}
\]
The equality follows from the continuity and strict increase asserted by that lemma.

Uniform linearization (4), covariance consistency (5), and the lower bound in (6) show that replacing the studentized linear term and its population standard deviations by the plug-in quantities changes the reported maximum by \(o_{P_n}(1)\).  The limit distribution in (10) is continuous, so the simultaneous coverage probability along the selected subsequence converges to \(1-\alpha\).  If convergence were not uniform, a sequence of laws would keep the coverage probability a fixed positive distance from \(1-\alpha\); compactness would produce a subsequence to which the preceding argument applies, a contradiction.  Therefore
\[
 \inf_{P\in\mathcal P_\kappa}
 P\{\theta_{J,\ell}\in I_{\ell,n}\text{ for every }\ell\in\mathcal L\}
 \longrightarrow1-\alpha.                                                \tag{11}
\]
Only positive reported marginal variances were used; neither \(\Sigma(p)\) nor its correlation matrix was inverted or assumed nonsingular.

open_obligations.what_is_open: For every constant-rank relative-interior stratum of the observed-law image of \(\mathcal M_{\mathrm{face}}\), construct a chart \(p(\zeta)\) whose differential exhausts that stratum's restricted tangent space, account for observationally equivalent latent representations, and evaluate for every reported direction \(a\) whether \(\{I-\Pi_{\operatorname{col}(S_P)}\}a^\top G_p\) is nonzero.
open_obligations.obstruction: The core supplies prospective symbols \(\zeta\) and \(S_P\), but it does not supply coordinates for cohort masses, type masses, initial laws, date-specific transition rows, common-kernel equalities, and support constraints. More importantly, \(\texttt{thm:active-frontier-recovery}\) leaves the allocation of date-\(1\) absorbers across latent types unidentified. The natural latent-primitive map is therefore noninjective, can have representation-dependent Jacobians, and may meet itself or change rank at boundary strata. A derivative at one latent representation is not thereby proved to span the tangent space of the observed-law image. Without an atlas or an equivalent finite system of observable equality constraints and a rank proof, \(\operatorname{col}(S_P)\) is undetermined; projecting onto a postulated space would assume the central step of the question.
open_obligations.attempted: A natural four-wave candidate parameterizes each legal observed cell \(p_{d,x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3}\) by cohort mass, known-\(J\) type masses, initial laws, and the \(H_j\), \(Q_j\), and \(R_j^d\) transition factors, subject to stochastic-row and common-kernel equalities. Differentiating this finite polynomial map gives a candidate Jacobian. This does not close the question: unreachable rows, label equivalences, and arbitrary type allocations among paths absorbed by date \(1\) yield nonunique primitive points above the same observed law, so the derivative at one representation has not been shown to span the tangent space of the entire observed-law stratum.
open_obligations.partial_result:
For any supplied \(C^1\) chart \(p(\zeta)\) on a fixed positive support \(\mathcal S_0\), let
\[
 W=\operatorname{diag}\{p_s:s\in\mathcal S_0\},\qquad
 A=\frac{\partial p(\zeta)}{\partial\zeta^\top},\qquad
 S=W^{-1}A.
\]
For a differentiable path \(\zeta_t\) through \(\zeta\), differentiation gives \(\dot p=A\dot\zeta\), so its observed-law score is \(h=W^{-1}\dot p=S\dot\zeta\).  If the chart has locally constant rank and its image is the whole chosen stratum, its score space is \(\operatorname{col}(S)\).  For any reported linear direction \(a\), put \(g_a(s)=a^\top G_p(s)\).  Weighted least squares then gives the computable projection
\[
 \Pi_{\operatorname{col}(S)}g_a
 =W^{-1}A(A^\top W^{-1}A)^\dagger A^\top g_a
\]
and the squared residual
\[
 \left\|(I-\Pi_{\operatorname{col}(S)})g_a\right\|_{L_2(P)}^2
 =g_a^\top Wg_a-(A^\top g_a)^\top
 (A^\top W^{-1}A)^\dagger(A^\top g_a).
\]
Thus the residual is nonzero exactly when the last display is positive, equivalently when \(g_a\notin\operatorname{col}(W^{-1}A)\).  This completes the projection calculation conditional on a valid full-stratum chart; construction and constant-rank certification of such a chart remain open.

prose_updates.tldr: For fixed known \(2\leq J\leq m\), four observed waves \(X_0,\ldots,X_3\) suffice. Four anchor slices determine the spectral basis, and \(2m-1\) fixed selected anchor-star minors transport it to every active state despite a common absorbing boundary. Projectors, stochastic row sums, a full-row-rank pseudoinverse, and full-predecessor-row transport recover active component sublaws, type contributions, at-risk effects, and the aggregate first-post ATT on the broad class; no date-\(1\) absorption upgrades these to full type shares and full conditional type effects. The resulting \(N_m=2\sum_{r=0}^{4}m^r\)-cell functional has an explicit saturated multinomial canonical gradient and guarded uniform Gaussian-multiplier bands under singular correlation. Restricted-model efficiency remains open.

project_justification.gap: Published short-panel Markov-mixture reconstruction and the closest transition-independence theorem impose rank, positivity, homogeneity, emission, or state-count conditions that do not deliver four-wave causal recovery at a common absorbing boundary. They also do not characterize the initial-absorber frontier, where full latent shares and conditional type effects can fail although active contributions and the aggregate remain identified.
project_justification.niche: For fixed known \(J\leq m\), fixed ex ante row and column selections, and an observable anchor star of \(2m-1\) nonsingular selected minors, four anchor slices identify a common spectral basis while the remaining star slices transport it across active states. Stochastic normalization handles exit, and absorption plus no anticipation makes date-\(1\) absorbers a zero-effect component.
project_justification.fill: The paper gives the explicit four-wave known-\(J\) projector, row-sum, pseudoinverse, and full-row transport map; proves the active-versus-full target frontier and a generic initial-absorber allocation counterexample; verifies an exact rational \(J=m=2\) witness; and derives the analytic saturated gradient plus guarded uniform multiplier bands.

sampling_model.design: Observational two-cohort four-wave panel \(O=(D,X_0,X_1,X_2,X_3)\), with adoption at date \(3\), a finite active state space of size \(m\), a common absorbing exit, fixed known \(2\leq J\leq m\), and possible date-\(1\) absorption in the headline class.
sampling_model.units: The data are \(n\) independent and identically distributed complete four-wave panels on the \(N_m=2\sum_{r=0}^{4}m^r\)-cell absorption-legal support; \(N_2=62\). A recorded fifth wave is unnecessary and may be marginalized out.
sampling_model.treatment: Cohort membership fixes the realized path; no anticipation holds through date \(2\), and units absorbed by date \(1\) have identical absorbed potential continuations through the first post-treatment date.
sampling_model.overlap: Both cohorts have positive probability. Positive active masses \(\alpha_j^d\), and hence positive full masses \(\pi_j^d\), follow from anchor-star nonsingularity rather than a separate type-overlap assumption.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: No nonparametric nuisance is fitted. Empirical frequencies on the fixed four-wave \(N_m\)-cell support feed the guarded analytic anchor-star recovery map.

prose_updates.related_work: Ahn and Kasahara (2026), Proposition 14 and Appendix A.4, provide the closest inverse-cancellation architecture, but their stated full-rank and positive-transition conditions exclude the common absorbing boundary; the present four-wave result is an excluded-boundary extension, not an application of their theorem. Higgins and Jochmans (2023) and Gupta, Kumar, and Vassilvitskii (2016) reconstruct Markov mixtures under their own homogeneity, component-rank, state-count, and nondegeneracy regimes; their scaling and label ideas are prior art, whereas the present theorem is causal, time-varying, and uses fixed known \(J\leq m\) selected anchor-star minors. Restricted hidden-Markov reconstruction results impose emission or other structural restrictions and do not prove the potential-path contribution identity here. Deaner and Ku (2026) study aggregate duration difference-in-differences rather than latent-type multi-state reconstruction. Bonhomme, Jochmans, and Robin (2017) motivate differentiating diagonalization estimators, while Chernozhukov, Chetverikov, and Kato (2013, 2015) are neighboring Gaussian-bootstrap and anti-concentration references. Rao and Risch (2026) are an interpretation consumer only: this paper does not claim their data satisfy the latent Markov, rank, support, or iid conditions. Restricted-model efficiency is left as an explicit open question.
prose_updates.interpretation:
The four-wave result separates the full type share \(\pi_j^d\), active share \(\alpha_j^d\), unnormalized contribution \(
u_j\), and at-risk effect \(\eta_j\). The \(2m-1\) anchor-star slices identify \(\alpha_j^d\), \(
u_j\), and \(\eta_j=
u_j/\alpha_j^1\), with positivity derived from nonsingularity. They cannot allocate already-absorbed zero-effect mass across latent labels, so full shares and full conditional effects need not be identified. If date-\(1\) absorption is absent, \(\pi_j^d=\alpha_j^d\) and \(	au_j=\eta_j\). The exact \(H_1,H_2,Q_1,Q_2,V_1,V_2\) witness verifies \(K^d= egin{pmatrix}29/5&-12/5\8/5&1/5\end{pmatrix}\), type exit effects \(-1/25\) and \(1/20\), and aggregate exit ATT \(1/200\); its all-exit reallocation exhibits the frontier. Rao and Risch's incumbent-firm setting motivates this decomposition but is not reanalyzed.
prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: The covariance \(\Sigma(p)\) is the canonical-gradient bound for the declared off-model continuation \(\Phi\) in the saturated four-wave finite-multinomial support-stratum model. The paper does not parameterize the smaller restricted Markov observed-law image, certify its score Jacobian on constant-rank strata, or claim its efficiency bound or an attaining estimator. The exact multiplier quantile is the mathematical object; a fixed Monte Carlo draw count requires separate approximation analysis. Weak eigengaps, changing selected-minor rank, unknown \(J\), adaptive anchor selection, clustered sampling, and approximate common kernels remain outside the result.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The paper proves a sufficient constructive frontier for fixed finite \(m\), known \(2\leq J\leq m\), four observed waves, fixed ex ante selected sets and anchor pairs, \(2m-1\) observable anchor-star nonsingularity conditions, distinct common cycle signatures, cohort overlap, type-conditional first-order Markov potential paths through date \(3\), no anticipation, absorption, and common untreated date-\(2\) and first-post kernels. It derives rather than assumes type positivity. The exact rational witness establishes nonvacuity, and the initial-absorber pair establishes the stated obstruction. The paper does not identify unknown type count, choose minors adaptively, cover weak or complex spectra, justify dependent-panel inference, or solve restricted-model efficiency. Full conditional type effects require no date-\(1\) absorption; the broad class identifies active sublaws, contributions, at-risk effects, and the aggregate.

statement_notes.justification: This is the field-level four-wave identification theorem: it transports a four-anchor spectral basis over all active states for fixed known \(J\leq m\), derives type positivity, and proves the aggregate-versus-full-conditional frontier.
statement_notes.gap: Adjacent reconstruction theorems do not combine a common absorbing boundary, \(2m-1\) selected anchor-star minors, four-wave time-varying causal paths, and the initial-absorber effect decomposition.
statement_notes.consumer: An analyst may marginalize any fifth wave and report latent-type contributions and the aggregate when the four-wave anchor-star guard passes, even if full latent allocation of already-exited units is unavailable.

statement_notes.justification: The corollary proves exactly what the observable no-date-\(1\)-absorption face adds: active masses become positive full masses and at-risk effects become full conditional type effects.
statement_notes.gap: Existing full-rank reconstruction does not establish this upgrade with a structurally singular common absorbing row and selected \(J\)-minors.
statement_notes.consumer: Full latent-type conditional effects are justified only after the observed four-wave panel verifies absence of absorption at the recovery cut.

statement_notes.justification: The four-wave generic allocation family certifies the sharp initial-absorber obstruction, while the rational \(J=m=2\) coupling verifies nonvacuity and every displayed normalization exactly.
statement_notes.gap: Absorbing-outcome difference-in-differences and generic mixture results do not isolate a four-wave reallocation of initial zero-effect absorbers that changes full conditional effects while preserving all active targets.
statement_notes.consumer: Researchers can use date-\(1\) exit as a falsifiable support diagnostic and avoid interpreting full conditional latent-type effects when initial absorbers are present.

statement_notes.justification: Analyticity makes the fixed-known-\(J\) four-wave recovery algorithm an explicit regular finite-multinomial estimator and exposes its saturated canonical gradient on each actual support stratum.
statement_notes.gap: Prior diagonalization asymptotics do not give the canonical gradient of this four-wave absorbing-boundary anchor-star, row-sum, pseudoinverse, and full-row transport map.
statement_notes.consumer: The four-wave delta-method covariance propagates estimated active masses and transported predecessor factors without introducing unidentified full shares.

statement_notes.justification: The theorem combines the buffered four-wave empirical guard with singular-correlation Gaussian-max quantile continuity for uniform simultaneous inference.
statement_notes.gap: Gaussian anti-concentration alone does not establish guard acceptance and uniform Taylor control for the rational four-wave recovery map.
statement_notes.consumer: Users can jointly report all \(J\) contribution vectors and their aggregate from four-wave panels despite structural covariance singularity.

statement_notes.justification: This is an explicit open question, not a theorem: restricted-model efficiency requires an observed-law parameterization, its finite score Jacobian, and a constant-rank projection calculation.
statement_notes.gap: The present paper derives only the saturated multinomial canonical gradient; it does not characterize the smaller restricted Markov tangent space.
statement_notes.consumer: A future restricted-likelihood analysis must compute \(S_P\) and test the residual projection before claiming a sharper bound or an attaining estimator.
